'''Willie Hobbs Moore''' (May 23, 1934 &ndash; March 14, 1994) was an [[African Americans|African American]] [[physicist]] and [[engineer]]. She is the first African American woman to earn a [[Doctor of Philosophy|PhD]] in [[physics]].<ref name=":0">{{Cite book|last=Mickens|first=Ronald E.|url=http://worldcat.org/oclc/191532647|title=Edward Bouchet : the first African-American doctorate|publisher=World Scientific|year=2002|isbn=978-981-02-4909-0|oclc=191532647}}</ref>

==Early life==
Willie Hobbs was born in [[Atlantic City]], [[New Jersey]], on May 23, 1934, to parents Bestie and Will Hobbs.<ref name=":0" /> Will Hobbs was a plumber and businessman and Bessie Hobbs was a housewife and local hotel employee. She had two sisters, Alice Doolin and Thelma Gordy. In high school, she was a straight A student with an aptitude for math and science.<ref name=":4">{{Cite web |last=Mickens |first=Ronald |date=September 2022 |title=The trailblazing career of Willie Hobbs Moore |url=https://pubs.aip.org/physicstoday/article/75/9/30/2845466/The-trailblazing-career-of-Willie-Hobbs-MooreThe |access-date=May 6, 2024 |archive-date=April 23, 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250423220403/https://pubs.aip.org/physicstoday/article/75/9/30/2845466/The-trailblazing-career-of-Willie-Hobbs-MooreThe |url-status=live }}</ref>

==Education==
In 1952, Hobbs moved to [[Ann Arbor]], [[Michigan]] where she attended the [[University of Michigan]] as a [[First-generation college students in the United States|first-generation college student]].<ref name=":1">{{Cite web|last=Sandberg|first=Ariel|date=February 17, 2017|title=Remembering trailblazer Willie Hobbs Moore, first African American woman to receive Ph.D.|url=https://news.engin.umich.edu/2017/02/remembering-trailblazer-willie-hobbs-moore-first-african-american-woman-to-receive-ph-d/|access-date=June 10, 2020|website=Michigan Engineering|language=en-US|archive-date=March 1, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210301133312/https://news.engin.umich.edu/2017/02/remembering-trailblazer-willie-hobbs-moore-first-african-american-woman-to-receive-ph-d/|url-status=dead}}</ref> At the University of Michigan, she became the first Black woman to earn a [[Bachelor of Science|bachelor of science]] in [[electrical engineering]] in 1958. Similarly, she became the first African-American woman to earn a [[Master of Science|master of science]] in electrical engineering in 1961.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Rosengren |first1=Paul Lief |title=IEEE-USA Releases New E-Book on Famous Women Engineers in History |url=https://insight.ieeeusa.org/articles/famous-women-engineers-in-history-willie-hobbs-moore/ |website=On Willie Hobbs Moore: Academic Barrier Breaker and Ford Engineer |publisher=IEEE - USA}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Willie Hobbs Moore (1934–1994): A First in EE and Physics |url=https://ece.engin.umich.edu/stories/willie-hobbs-moore |publisher=University of Michigan |access-date=6 October 2026}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book|last=Smith, Jessie Carney.|url=http://worldcat.org/oclc/818851419|title=Black firsts : 4,000 ground-breaking & pioneering historical events|date=2013|publisher=Visible Ink Press|isbn=978-1-57859-424-5|oclc=818851419|archive-date=June 10, 2020|access-date=June 10, 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200610233705/https://www.worldcat.org/oclc/818851419|url-status=live}}</ref> 

In 1972, she earned a [[doctorate]] in physics from the University of Michigan, making her the first African American woman to receive a PhD in physics from an American university.<ref name=":1" /><ref>{{Cite web |title=Black On Campus » Timeline: Black Firsts in Higher Education |url=https://blackoncampus.com/timeline/ |access-date=2026-02-03}}</ref> Her doctoral [[thesis]], ''A Vibrational Analysis of Chlorides'',<ref name="thesis">{{cite web |last1=Moore |first1=Willie Hobbs |title=A Vibrational Analysis of Secondary Chlorides |url=https://search.lib.umich.edu/catalog/record/002151361?query=A+Vibrational+Analysis+of+Secondary+Chlorides&library=All+libraries |website=Dissertation, Ph.D. Thesis |publisher=University of Michigan |access-date=February 26, 2021 |archive-date=August 11, 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240811072225/https://search.lib.umich.edu/catalog/record/002151361?query=A+Vibrational+Analysis+of+Secondary+Chlorides&library=All+libraries |url-status=live }}</ref> was completed under the supervision of [[Spectroscopy|spectroscopist]] Dr. Samuel Krimm.<ref>{{Cite web|date=February 2, 2018|title=Willie Hobbs Moore|url=https://www.nsbp.org/en/cev/94|access-date=June 10, 2020|website=The National Society of Black Physicists|archive-date=June 10, 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200610233649/https://www.nsbp.org/en/cev/94|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Samuel Krimm |url=https://lsa.umich.edu/physics/people/emeritus/skrimm.html |website=University of Michigan Physics}}</ref> Moores thesis focused on the vibrations of secondary chlorides for polyvinyl-chloride polymers. In her work, Moore calculated the vibrational modes of many nonlinear organic molecules that contain secondary chloride atoms. Her goal was to complete a potential field that could be used in normal coordinate analyses to predict the vibrational modes of all secondary chlorides. Next, Moore used vibrational spectroscopy to determine the structure of PVCs. With her data Moore obtained a force field for secondary chlorides and used it to calculate the vibrational frequencies of crystalline PVC.<ref name=":4" /> 

After receiving her doctorate, Moore worked at the University of Michigan in the department of physics and the Macromolecular Research Center as a lecturer and research scientist until 1977, continuing spectroscopic work on [[protein]]s.<ref name=":2">{{Cite web |title=Willie Hobbs Moore {{!}} UM WISE |url=https://wise.umich.edu/?page_id=63#AwardsFAQ |access-date=February 22, 2021 |website=University of Michigan Women in Science and Engineering |archive-date=July 7, 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240707125449/https://wise.umich.edu/?page_id=63#AwardsFAQ |url-status=dead }}</ref> In the five years following her dissertation, she published more than thirty papers with Krimm and collaborators,<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Moore |first1=W.H. |last2=Ching |first2=J.H.C. |last3=Warrier |first3=A.V.R. |last4=Krimm |first4=S. |date=October 1973 |title=Assignment of torsion and low frequency bending vibrations of secondary chlorides |journal=Spectrochimica Acta Part A: Molecular Spectroscopy |volume=29 |issue=10 |pages=1847–1858 |bibcode=1973AcSpA..29.1847M |doi=10.1016/0584-8539(73)80169-2 |hdl-access=free |hdl=2027.42/33808}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Rabolt |first1=J. F. |last2=Moore |first2=W. H. |last3=Krimm |first3=S. |date=September 1977 |title=Vibrational Analysis of Peptides, Polypeptides, and Proteins. 3. α-Poly(L-alanine) |journal=Macromolecules |volume=10 |issue=5 |pages=1065–1074 |bibcode=1977MaMol..10.1065R |doi=10.1021/ma60059a034 |pmid=916733}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Moore |first1=W. H. |last2=Krimm |first2=S. |date=1 December 1975 |title=Transition dipole coupling in Amide I modes of βpolypeptides |journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences |volume=72 |issue=12 |pages=4933–4935 |bibcode=1975PNAS...72.4933M |doi=10.1073/pnas.72.12.4933 |pmc=388847 |pmid=16592297 |doi-access=free}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Hsu |first1=S. L. |last2=Moore |first2=W. H. |last3=Krimm |first3=S. |date=October 1975 |title=A vibrational analysis of crystalline trans‐1,4‐polybutadiene |journal=Journal of Applied Physics |volume=46 |issue=10 |pages=4185–4193 |bibcode=1975JAP....46.4185H |doi=10.1063/1.321430 |hdl-access=free |hdl=2027.42/69708}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Moore |first1=W.H. |last2=Krimm |first2=S. |date=December 1973 |title=A complete general valence force field for secondary chlorides |journal=Spectrochimica Acta Part A: Molecular Spectroscopy |volume=29 |issue=12 |pages=2025–2042 |bibcode=1973AcSpA..29.2025M |doi=10.1016/0584-8539(73)80061-3 |hdl-access=free |hdl=2027.42/33779}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Moore |first1=W. H. |last2=Krimm |first2=S. |date=November 1973 |title=Calculated intermolecular interactions in secondary chlorides |journal=The Journal of Chemical Physics |volume=59 |issue=9 |pages=5195–5196 |bibcode=1973JChPh..59.5195M |doi=10.1063/1.1680738 |hdl-access=free |hdl=2027.42/71083}}</ref> in a variety of journals, including the ''[[Journal of Molecular Spectroscopy]]'', ''[[The Journal of Chemical Physics]]'', and the ''[[Journal of Applied Physics]].''<ref name=":1" /> Additionally, Moore and Yuin Wu published "Quality Engineering" in the American Supplier Institute in 1986.<ref name=":5">{{Cite web |last=Dartis |first=Michelle |date=2018-03-11 |title=Willie Hobbs Moore (1934 -1994) • |url=https://www.blackpast.org/african-american-history/moore-willie-hobbs-1934-1994/ |access-date=2024-05-06 |language=en-US |archive-date=June 14, 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250614080457/https://www.blackpast.org/african-american-history/moore-willie-hobbs-1934-1994/ |url-status=live }}</ref>

== Career ==
From 1961 to 1962 Moore worked at a Junior engineer at Bendix Aerospace Systems, where she calculated the radiation from various types of plasmas and also wrote proposals. From 1962-1963 Moore took a job at Barnes Engineering Company where she worked on approximating the IR radiation from wakes of space reentry vehicles. By the end of 1963, Moore was working at Senor Dynamics as a theoretical analyst of stress-optical devices.<ref name=":4" /> 

Next Moore was a research associate at the Institute of Science and Technology at the University of Michigan where she modeled optical hypersonic wakes and certified existing flow-field models. In 1967, Moore began working at KMS Industries as a system analyst where she supported optics design staff and established computer requirements for optics. Then Moore worked as a senior analyst at Datamax Corp in 1968.<ref name=":4" />

In 1977, Moore was hired by [[Ford Motor Company]] as an assembly engineer.<ref name="obituary">{{cite news |last1=Grantham |first1=Russell |date=March 15, 1994 |title=Scholar, tutor, pioneering black woman dies |url=http://oldnews.aadl.org/aa_news_19940315-scholar_tutor_pioneering_black_woman_dies |access-date=February 17, 2015 |work=Ann Arbor News |archive-date=December 20, 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161220091710/http://oldnews.aadl.org/aa_news_19940315-scholar_tutor_pioneering_black_woman_dies |url-status=live }}</ref> Moore expanded Ford's use of Japanese engineering and manufacturing methods in the 1980s.<ref name=":0" /> She did this in part by writing a technical paper which communicated the concepts of Japanese engineer [[Genichi Taguchi]] as working design methods for practical use.<ref name=":3">{{Cite news|last=Grantham|first=Russell|date=February 4, 1991|title=A driving force at Ford|work=Ann Arbor News|url=https://aadl.org/aa_news_19910204-a_driving_force_at_ford|access-date=June 10, 2020}}</ref> Moore went on to become an executive at Ford; in this position she oversaw the warranty department of the automobile assembly.<ref name=":5" /> 

In January 1991, ''[[Ebony (magazine)|Ebony]]'' magazine named Moore as one of their 100 "Most Promising Black Women in Corporate America".<ref name=":3" />

==Personal life==
On August 17, 1963, Willie Hobbs Moore married Sidney Moore and they were married for thirty years. Sidney Moore has a bachelor of science from Jackson State University in Mississippi and master of science in educational psychology from the University of Michigan.<ref name=":4" /> Sidney Moore worked at Michigan Neuropsychiatric Institute for 38 years and retired in 1997. They had two children, Dorian Moore, [[Doctor of Medicine|M.D.]] and Christopher Moore RN. Moore has 3 grandchildren, Sydney Padgett, William Hobbs Moore, and C. Jackson Moore.

According to firsthand interviews with family members, Krimm, former students and mentees Moore was “highly intelligent, witty, empathetic, and kindhearted with a mild New Jersey accent”.<ref name=":4" /> 

Moore was a tutor at the Saturday African-American Academy in Ann Arbor, a community program for teaching science and mathematics to students in grades 5–12.<ref name=":0" /> She was also a member of [[The Links]], Incorporated.<ref name=":0" /> Additionally, Moore was a member of the [[Delta Sigma Theta]] sorority and also a member of the Bethel African Methodist Episcopal Church. Moore was also a chairwomen of the Juanita S. Woods Scholarship fund and a part of the Jill and Jack of America organization.<ref name=":5" />

Moore died of cancer in her Ann Arbor home on March 14, 1994.<ref name=":0" />

== Legacy ==
In Moore's honor, the University of Michigan Women in Science and Engineering office established the Willie Hobbs Moore Awards, ''created to honor'' faculty, staff, and students who demonstrate excellence promoting equity in STEM. Four awards are given out at the ceremony'':'' the ''Willie Hobbs Moore Achievement Award'' for achievements in [[Science, technology, engineering, and mathematics|STEM]], the ''Sister Mary Ambrosia Fitzgerald Mentoring Award'' for exemplary mentorship of STEM students, the ''[[Claudia Alexander|Claudia Joan Alexander]] Trailblazer Award'' for innovation in STEM education, and the ''Cinda Sue Davis STEM Equity Leadership Award'' for excellence promoting diversity, equity, and inclusion across a successful career.<ref name=":2" /><ref>{{Cite web |title=Willie Hobbs Moore Awards – Women in Science and Engineering |url=https://wise.umich.edu/willie-hobbs-moore-awards/ |access-date=2026-02-03 |language=en-US}}</ref>

The University of Michigan department of Electrical & Computer Engineering invites alumni from underrepresented groups to give their ''ECE Willie Hobbs Moore Alumni Lecture'', a lecture series aimed at bringing together professional leaders with the university community.<ref>{{Cite web |title=ECE Willie Hobbs Moore Distinguished Alumni Lecture |url=https://ece.engin.umich.edu/events/distinguished-lectures/ece-willie-hobbs-moore-distinguished-alumni-lecture// |access-date=2023-08-21 |website=Electrical and Computer Engineering |language=en-US}}</ref>
